Nissan has a laundry list of mothballed nameplates and concept cars enthusiasts cared about. When asked if the Maxima would return Ponz said, “Well, you know what I’d like to bring back before a Maxima is a Silvia.”

items.title: Hyundai N Vision 74 Production Plans Are Dead, For Now
items.summary:
Hyundai’s N Vision 74 ground the automotive internet to a halt on a Friday in July four years ago. With that concept, the automaker recast one of the most consequential models of its history, the Giugiaro-penned, 1974 Pony, into a modern supercar with turbofans and an unapologetically big wing. Enthusiasts have waited to see it get the green light for production ever since. To hear a Hyundai executive tell it, that ship has likely already sailed.

Rumblings have come and gone, and reports of trademark renewals have kept a glimmer of hope alive, but the beat has gone cold. For unfortunately good reason, as Hyundai Design Center boss Simon Loasby explained to The Drive during the media preview for the 2027 Elantra . We asked him if the N Vision 74 would ever get produced, and his answer was predictable, but nevertheless disappointing.

“At the moment, no,” Loasby said. “We were really on it. We had the production clay model of it and the exterior, interior, and so on. It comes down to the maths of how you judge what the business case is. And that if you’re very tight with the business case on only that car, the volumes of that car and the impact, you got no chance. If you open it to the overall brand-raising profile value of that, you have a bigger chance. But as yet, [no].”

items.title: Here’s Why Scout Isn’t Doing Removable Doors and Roofs Yet
items.summary:
Scout might be staking its claim as the electric truck brand for serious off-roaders and explorers who need ladder-frame power and dependability, but it’s not necessarily angling to replace the Wrangler and Bronco on their turf.

During his appearance on The Drivecast , Scout CEO Scott Keogh said that removable doors and roof panels are not something the revived brand is planning—at least, not yet.

“We’ve been interacting with the Scout community—actually, we showed the first concept to the Scout OGs before we showed the journalists,” Keogh said. “We invited them down to Dallas, and look—the number one thing we wanted to do was build an authentic, credible, rugged vehicle. Hence body-on-frame, hence solid rear axle, hence mechanical switches and door handles, all those kind of things. So, 100% we’ve achieved that. We will not do removable doors and removable tops on the Traveler as we know it.”

Scout Motors 

Keogh said if Scout props up another model, a three-row SUV would be a likely candidate. Given that, the potential for a more modular SUV with optional panels, in the vein of the Wrangler and Bronco, seems like a far-off consideration. But he didn’t shut the door.

The trans itself is a Tremec unit, but it was a tuner shop in Texas called Peitz Performance Tunes that actually cracked the code to make it functional. I caught up with Alex Peitz, the owner and tuner there, to find out how he worked his magic and when consumers will be able to buy their own C8 manual conversion kits.

First, I asked him what the car’s like to drive. And even though we have Hurd’s impressions (linked above), Peitz has a lot more miles on it, including highway blasts and running full noise on track.

“Like I tell everybody, it’s a transformative experience. It’s impossible to drive this car and not have a smile on your face. Actually, the president of Shelby American drove it on Sunday. items.title: VW Dealers Are Suing Scout. Its CEO Is Invoking the Consitution
items.summary:
Scout Motors is part of Volkswagen Group thanks to the German automaker acquiring the rights when it bought Navistar in 2021, but the “startup” automaker is adamant it is its own company. To that point, it plans to go the direct sales route when it starts delivering vehicles in 2028. Naturally, Volkswagen and Audi dealerships are irate and suing .

On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Scout Motors President and CEO Scott Keogh exclusively told The Drive , “There is only plan A, and plan A is to execute it direct to consumer, ” when asked what Scout’s plan B if the direct sales route doesn’t work out. Keogh also argued that interstate commerce is protected by the Constitution, and that no judge can tell a consumer they can’t buy a Scout.

You can listen to Keogh address Scout going the direct sales route and the reasons why below.

“There is only plan A, and plan A is to execute it direct to consumer. And the reason there’s no plan B in my mind is, one, it’s strategically right,” Keogh said. 

Addressing why the direct sales route is strategically right, Keogh said, “In this environment, you wanna have a relationship directly with the customer. You wanna have direct control of the data. And in the world of AI, I promise you, you wanna have to do that. When you have someone’s agent buying a car from another person’s agent, spiraled across thousands of dealerships, it’s, it’s gonna be chaos . So 100% is the right strategy.”

items.title: This School Bus Was Repurposed Into the Ultimate Hay Mover—And It Runs Backwards
items.summary:
There are a lot of fantastic tools out there, and I’m convinced some of the best are those you build yourself . If you have a super specific job to do, it’s not a bad idea to forge or fabricate an arsenal of super specialized equipment to get it done. I feel like Dallas Henry would agree, as he has done it time and again—perhaps most notably with a 25-year-old school bus that now operates as a hay loader .

It’s a 2001 International 3800 with a venerable DT466 diesel engine. And while that compression-ignition lump is still under the hood, it isn’t at the front of the loader bus; it’s at the back. That’s because Henry flipped its orientation around so that the ring gear is on the opposite side of the pinion gear, reversing the drive direction. The Allison automatic and auxiliary transmission retain all of their forward gears; the machine simply drives the other way.

“If all tie rods and steering components are right, it works real good,” Henry told me. “Top speed was 36 mph. I recently put a newer rear end that accepts the hub pilot wheels. The gear ratio is a little lower. Haven’t had it on the road to tell. I usually haul it at distances.”

Dallas Henry 

In the field is where this rig really shines. The front-end loader is an Art’s Way 5000 unit built in the late ’60s or early ’70s, originally intended for articulated 4×4 tractors. Henry fabbed it to fit the bus instead, and now he has a machine that will lift as much as 9,000 pounds—more hay than he could realistically skewer with the forks.
